studies.Study: García-Closas R et al. (2007) [PMID: 17596928] — estimate 1 · Mixed
studies.Reference: Food, nutrient and heterocyclic amine intake and the risk of bladder cancer.
studies.Title: Food, nutrient and heterocyclic amine intake and the risk of bladder cancer.
studies.Authors: García-Closas R, García-Closas M, Kogevinas M, Malats N, Silverman D, Serra C, Tardón A, Carrato A, Castaño-Vinyals G, Dosemeci M, Moore L, Rothman N, Sinha R
studies.Population: incident bladder cancer cases and controls in Spain

sample_size.excerpt: The association between diet and bladder cancer risk was evaluated among 912 incident bladder cancer cases and 873 controls in Spain.
sample_size.location: abstract; total_n derived from reported group counts 912 + 873 = 1785

cases.excerpt: The association between diet and bladder cancer risk was evaluated among 912 incident bladder cancer cases and 873 controls in Spain.

effect_size.excerpt: Meat or fish intake, their cooking methods or level of doneness, or heterocyclic amine intakes were not significantly associated with risk. Intake of folate, other B-vitamins (B12, B6, B2) and retinol was also associated with a reduced risk, the strongest associations being for vitamin B6 (0.6 (0.4, 0.8) p trend=0.0006) and retinol (0.6 (0.4-0.9) p trend=0.004).

confidence_interval.excerpt: Intake of folate, other B-vitamins (B12, B6, B2) and retinol was also associated with a reduced risk, the strongest associations being for vitamin B6 (0.6 (0.4, 0.8) p trend=0.0006) and retinol (0.6 (0.4-0.9) p trend=0.004).
